Normal distribution
A normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution that describes the population that has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) forms a bell-shaped curve.

Bell-shaped and symmetric

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders — Part 3
text:
Normal distribution
It has the closed mathematical form that defines the normal distribution:
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\!\left( -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
\]

The \(f(x)\) there refers to the density function. Some textbooks denotes the density function as \(f_X(x)\).


The random variable for this distribution \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)\) (reads as “X follows the normal distribution with parameters mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\)”).

The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule)
The Empirical Rule (also called the 68-95-99.7 Rule) tells us what percentage of data falls within certain distances from the mean in a normal distribution.


68% Rule
Approximately 68% of data falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean:
\[\mu - \sigma \leq X \leq \mu + \sigma\]

95% Rule
Approximately 95% of data falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean:
\[\mu - 2\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma\]

99.7% Rule
Approximately 99.7% of data falls within 3 standard deviations of the mean:
\[\mu - 3\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 3\sigma\]

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders — Part 3
text:
Practice Problem
Scenario: Heights of adult males in a population are normally distributed with a mean of 175 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm.
Questions:

What percentage of men have heights between 167 cm and 183 cm?
What percentage of men are taller than 191 cm?
If a man is 159 cm tall, how many standard deviations is he from the mean?
Would a height of 159 cm be considered unusual? Why or why not?


Solutions:

167 to 183 cm = \(\mu \pm 1\sigma\). It should be 68%
191 cm = \(\mu + 2\sigma\)

Beyond \(2\sigma\) above mean
\((100\% - 95\%) / 2\) = 2.5%

\(z = \frac{159 - 175}{8} = \frac{-16}{8} = -2\) — 2 standard deviations below
Yes, unusual because it’s exactly \(2\sigma\) below the mean (only 2.5% are this short or shorter)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
What is Statistics?
Definition
Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting, and presenting data. Used in research, business, science, and everyday decision-making

Two kinds of statistics:


Descriptive Statistics: The way to summarize and describe data (mean, median, mode, graphs)
Inferential Statistics: Meticulous way to make generalizations, i.e. predictions or inferences, about a population based on sample data

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
What is Probability?
Definition
Probability is the measure of the likelihood that an event will occur.

Expressed as a decimal number between 0 and 1 (or 0% to 100%)
\(P(E) = 0\) means the event is impossible
\(P(E) = 1\) means the event is certain
Helps us make predictions about random events

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Calculating Basic Probability
Formula for Probability
\[P(\text{Event}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total number of possible outcomes}}=\frac{x}{n}\]

Example: Rolling a die
What is the probability of rolling a 4 in a die?

Favorable outcomes: {4} \(\rightarrow\) 1 outcome
Total outcomes: \(\{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6\}\) \(\rightarrow\) 6 outcomes
\(P(\text{rolling a 4}) = \frac{1}{6}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Sample Space
Definition
A sample space (S) is the collection or set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

Represented using the symbol “S” or \(\Omega\) in some textbooks
Contains all outcomes that could occur
Can be finite or infinite


Examples:


Tossing a coin: \(S = \{H, T\}\)
Rolling a die: \(S = \{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6\}\)
Tossing two coins: \(S = \{HH,\ HT,\ TH,\ TT\}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events
Definition
An event is a subset of possible outcomes from the sample space.

Can be a single outcome or multiple outcomes
Denoted by capital letters (A, B, C)








Important


When you calculate the probability of the event \(P(E)\), it is ALWAYS a decimal number, a fractional number, ranges from 0 to 1.
For example:
When tossing a coin, what’s the probability of getting heads? There should be two outcomes: getting a head & getting a tail . The sample space would be: \(S=\{H,\ T\}\) And the event A is getting head Thus, \(x=1;\ n=2\), and the probability would be:
\[P(A)=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\]

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events
Definition

An event is any subset of possible outcomes in the sample space \(\Omega\).
Compound event: contains two or more outcomes (e.g., “rolling an even number”)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Calculating Probability of Events
Practice Problem:
A bag contains 5 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 2 green balls.

What is the probability of drawing a red ball?
What is the probability of drawing a blue or green ball?
What is the probability of NOT drawing a red ball?



\(P(\text{red}) = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}\)
\(P(\text{blue or green}) = \frac{3}{10} + \frac{2}{10} = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}\)
\(P(\text{not red}) = 1 - P(\text{red}) = 1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events

Mutually Exclusive (Disjoint) Events
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive if they have no outcomes in common:
\[A \cap B = \emptyset\]
Consequence for probabilities:
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\] (no overlap to double-count)
Classic example – Die roll

\(A\): Rolling an even number \(\{2,\ 4,\ 6\}\)
\(B\): Rolling an odd number \(\{1,\ 3,\ 5\}\)

\(\rightarrow\) \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) \(\rightarrow\) mutually exclusive

Another example: Drawing one card

\(A\): Drawing a heart
\(B\): Drawing a spade

\(\rightarrow\) also mutually exclusive

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events

Non-Mutually Exclusive Events
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are non-mutually exclusive if they share at least one outcome:
\[A \cap B \neq \emptyset\]
Addition rule becomes:
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\] (we subtract the overlap so it’s not counted twice)
Die roll example

\(A\): Rolling an even number: \(\{2,\ 4,\ 6\}\)
\(B\): Rolling a number $ >4 : {5, 6}$

\(\rightarrow\) \(A \cap B = \{6\} \neq \emptyset\) \(\rightarrow\) not mutually exclusive
\(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Random Variables
Definition
A random variable is a function that assigns a numerical value to each outcome in the sample space of a random experiment.
Notation: We use capital letters (X, Y, Z) for random variables
How it works:

Perform a random experiment \(\rightarrow\) get outcomes in sample space \(S\)
The random variable \(X\) maps each outcome to a number
We can then calculate probabilities: \(P(X = x)\)


Intuition: Tossing two coins

Sample space: \(S = \{HH,\ HT,\ TH,\ TT\}\)
Let \(X\) = number of heads
Mapping: \(HH \rightarrow 2\), \(HT \rightarrow 1\), \(TH \rightarrow 1\), \(TT \rightarrow 0\)
So \(X\) can be 0, 1, or 2
\(P(X = 1) = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\) (since HT and TH both give 1 head)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Random Variables


Definition
A random variable is a function that assigns numerical values to outcomes of a random experiment.

Maps outcomes to real numbers
Denoted by capital letters (X, Y, Z)
Can be discrete or continuous


Example
Rolling a die: \(X = \text{number shown}\)

\(X\) can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6
Each outcome has equal probability
\(P(X = k) = \frac{1}{6}; k \in {\{1,2,3,4,5,6}\}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Types of Random Variables


Discrete Random Variables
Takes on countable values

Key Property: Can list all discrete possible values


Examples:


Number of heads in 10 coin flips
Number of students absent
Number of cars passing by
Number of balls drawn in an urn


Continuous Random Variables
Takes on uncountably infinite values

Key Property: Any value in an interval is possible


Examples:


Height of students
Time until next bus arrives
Temperature at noon
Waiting time

A probability distribution assigns probabilities to each possible value.
Requirements:

\(0 \leq P(X = x) \leq 1\) for all \(x\)
\(\sum_{x}^{\infty}P(X = x) = 1\) (sum over all possible values)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Expected Value (Mean)
The expected value E(X) is the average value we expect from a random variable.
Formula
\[E(X) = \sum_{i}^{\infty} x_i \cdot P(X = x_i)\]

Example: Rolling a die
\[E(X) = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 4 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 5 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 6 \cdot \frac{1}{6}\]


\[E(X) = \frac{21}{6} = 3.5\]

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Variance and Standard Deviation
Variance \(\sigma^2\)

Measures how spread out the values are from the mean.
\[\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]\] \[= \sum_{i} (x_i - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_i)\]
where \(\mu = E(X)\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Variance and Standard Deviation


Variance \(\sigma^2\)
Measures how spread out the values are from the mean.
\[\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]\] \[= \sum_{i} (x_i - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_i)\]
where \(\mu = E(X)\)

Standard Deviation \(\sigma\)
The square root of variance (same units as X).
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\]
Interpretation:

Small \(\sigma\): values clustered near mean
Large \(\sigma\): values spread out

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
section: Where Do All These Distributions Come From?
text:

Many real-life situations follow repeatable patterns. When we study those patterns carefully, we discover a handful of probability distributions that keep showing up again and again.

What is Statistics?
Definition
Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting, and presenting data. Used in research, business, science, and everyday decision-making

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
What is Probability?
Definition
Probability is the measure of the likelihood that an event will occur.

Expressed as a decimal number between 0 and 1 (or 0% to 100%)
\(P(E) = 0\) means the event is impossible
\(P(E) = 1\) means the event is certain
Helps us make predictions about random events

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Calculating Basic Probability
Formula for Probability
\[P(\text{Event}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total number of possible outcomes}}=\frac{x}{n}\]

Example: Rolling a die
What is the probability of rolling a 4 in a die?

Favorable outcomes: {4} \(\rightarrow\) 1 outcome
Total outcomes: \(\{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6\}\) \(\rightarrow\) 6 outcomes
\(P(\text{rolling a 4}) = \frac{1}{6}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Sample Space
Definition
A sample space (S) is the collection or set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

Represented using the symbol “S” or \(\Omega\) in some textbooks
Contains all outcomes that could occur
Can be finite or infinite


Examples:


Tossing a coin: \(S = \{H, T\}\)
Rolling a die: \(S = \{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6\}\)
Tossing two coins: \(S = \{HH,\ HT,\ TH,\ TT\}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events
Definition
An event is a subset of possible outcomes from the sample space.

Can be a single outcome or multiple outcomes
Denoted by capital letters (A, B, C)








Important


When you calculate the probability of the event \(P(E)\), it is ALWAYS a decimal number, a fractional number, ranges from 0 to 1.
For example:
When tossing a coin, what’s the probability of getting heads? There should be two outcomes: getting a head & getting a tail . The sample space would be: \(S=\{H,\ T\}\) And the event A is getting head Thus, \(x=1;\ n=2\), and the probability would be:
\[P(A)=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\]

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events
Definition

An event is any subset of possible outcomes in the sample space \(\Omega\).
Compound event: contains two or more outcomes (e.g., “rolling an even number”)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Calculating Probability of Events
Practice Problem:
A bag contains 5 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 2 green balls.

What is the probability of drawing a red ball?
What is the probability of drawing a blue or green ball?
What is the probability of NOT drawing a red ball?



\(P(\text{red}) = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}\)
\(P(\text{blue or green}) = \frac{3}{10} + \frac{2}{10} = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}\)
\(P(\text{not red}) = 1 - P(\text{red}) = 1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events

Mutually Exclusive (Disjoint) Events
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive if they have no outcomes in common:
\[A \cap B = \emptyset\]
Consequence for probabilities:
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\] (no overlap to double-count)
Classic example – Die roll

\(A\): Rolling an even number \(\{2,\ 4,\ 6\}\)
\(B\): Rolling an odd number \(\{1,\ 3,\ 5\}\)

\(\rightarrow\) \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) \(\rightarrow\) mutually exclusive

Another example: Drawing one card

\(A\): Drawing a heart
\(B\): Drawing a spade

\(\rightarrow\) also mutually exclusive

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Events

Non-Mutually Exclusive Events
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are non-mutually exclusive if they share at least one outcome:
\[A \cap B \neq \emptyset\]
Addition rule becomes:
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\] (we subtract the overlap so it’s not counted twice)
Die roll example

\(A\): Rolling an even number: \(\{2,\ 4,\ 6\}\)
\(B\): Rolling a number $ >4 : {5, 6}$

\(\rightarrow\) \(A \cap B = \{6\} \neq \emptyset\) \(\rightarrow\) not mutually exclusive
\(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Random Variables
Definition
A random variable is a function that assigns a numerical value to each outcome in the sample space of a random experiment.
Notation: We use capital letters (X, Y, Z) for random variables
How it works:

Perform a random experiment \(\rightarrow\) get outcomes in sample space \(S\)
The random variable \(X\) maps each outcome to a number
We can then calculate probabilities: \(P(X = x)\)


Intuition: Tossing two coins

Sample space: \(S = \{HH,\ HT,\ TH,\ TT\}\)
Let \(X\) = number of heads
Mapping: \(HH \rightarrow 2\), \(HT \rightarrow 1\), \(TH \rightarrow 1\), \(TT \rightarrow 0\)
So \(X\) can be 0, 1, or 2
\(P(X = 1) = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\) (since HT and TH both give 1 head)

Expected Value (Mean)
The expected value E(X) is the average value we expect from a random variable.
Formula
\[E(X) = \sum_{i}^{\infty} x_i \cdot P(X = x_i)\]

Example: Rolling a die
\[E(X) = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 4 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 5 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 6 \cdot \frac{1}{6}\]

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Variance and Standard Deviation
Variance \(\sigma^2\)

Measures how spread out the values are from the mean.
\[\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]\] \[= \sum_{i} (x_i - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_i)\]
where \(\mu = E(X)\)

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders
text:
Variance and Standard Deviation


Variance \(\sigma^2\)
Measures how spread out the values are from the mean.
\[\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]\] \[= \sum_{i} (x_i - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_i)\]
where \(\mu = E(X)\)

Standard Deviation \(\sigma\)
The square root of variance (same units as X).
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\]
Interpretation:

Small \(\sigma\): values clustered near mean
Large \(\sigma\): values spread out

A normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution that describes the population that has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) forms a bell-shaped curve.

Bell-shaped and symmetric

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders — Part 2

Normal distribution
It has its own closed mathematical form that defines the normal distribution:
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\!\left( -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
\]

The \(f(x)\) there refers to the density function. Some textbooks denotes the density function as \(f_X(x)\).


The random variable for this distribution \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)\) (reads as “X follows the normal distribution with parameters mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\)”).

The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule)
The Empirical Rule (also called the 68-95-99.7 Rule) tells us what percentage of data falls within certain distances from the mean in a normal distribution.


68% Rule
Approximately 68% of data falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean:
\[\mu - \sigma \leq X \leq \mu + \sigma\]

95% Rule
Approximately 95% of data falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean:
\[\mu - 2\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma\]

99.7% Rule
Approximately 99.7% of data falls within 3 standard deviations of the mean:
\[\mu - 3\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 3\sigma\]

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 3
text:
Real-World Example 1
Problem: Test scores are normally distributed with \(\mu = 75\) and \(\sigma = 10\). What is the probability that a randomly selected student scored less than 85?

Solution:
Step 1: Convert to z-score \[z = \frac{85 - 75}{10} = \frac{10}{10} = 1.00\]
Step 2: Look up \(z = 1.00\) in table. This will be 0.8413
Interpretation: \(84.13\%\) of students scored less than 85

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 3
text:
Real-World Example 2
Problem: Heights of adult men are normally distributed with \(\mu = 175\) cm and \(\sigma = 8\) cm. What percentage of men are taller than 183 cm?

Solution:
Step 1: Convert to z-score \[z = \frac{183 - 175}{8} = \frac{8}{8} = 1.00\]
Step 2: \[P(Z > 1.00) = 1 - P(Z < 1.00) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587\]
Interpretation: \(15.87\%\) of men are taller than 183 cm

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 3
text:
Real-World Example 3
Problem: Battery life is normally distributed with \(\mu = 400\) hours and \(\sigma = 50\) hours. What is the probability a battery lasts between 350 and 450 hours?

Solution:
Step 1: Convert both values to z-scores \[z_1 = \frac{350 - 400}{50} = -1.00, \quad z_2 = \frac{450 - 400}{50} = 1.00\]
Step 2: \[P(-1.00 < Z < 1.00) = 0.8413 - 0.1587 = 0.6826\]
Interpretation: \(68.26\%\) of batteries last between 350 and 450 hours

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 3
text:
Practice Problem 2
Problem: Your monthly electric bill has \(\mu = 1500\) and \(\sigma = 120\). What is the probability you’ll pay between 1380 and 1740?

Solution:
\[z_1 = \frac{1380 - 1500}{120} = -1.00, \quad z_2 = \frac{1740 - 1500}{120} = 2.00\]
Answer: \(P(-1.00 < Z < 2.00) = 0.9772 - 0.1587 = \mathbf{0.8185}\) or 81.85%

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 3
text:
Example: Finding X
Problem: Test scores are normally distributed with \(\mu = 70\) and \(\sigma = 12\). What score represents the 90th percentile?

Solution:
Step 1: Find z-score where \(P(Z < z) = 0.90\)

Looking through the table, \(z \approx \mathbf{1.28}\)

Step 2: Calculate x
\[x = 70 + (1.28)(12) = 70 + 15.36 = 85.36\]
Interpretation: A score of approximately 85.36 (around 85 or 86) represents the 90th percentile. Which means you got a better score of 85 than 90% of others, with only 10% scoring higher.

To Calculate Probability from the Normal Distribution
This is how you calculate the cumulative probability:
\[
P(z_1 \leq Z \leq z_2) = F(z) = \int_{z_1}^{z_2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\left( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right) dz
\]
The parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are already cancelled since \(\mu=0\) and \(\sigma = 1\).

Do not attempt to calculate this. We need tools to find exact probabilities!

text:
What is Statistical Inference?
Statistical inference is the process of drawing conclusions about a population based on data from a sample.
Why do we need it?

We can rarely measure an entire population
Instead, we collect a sample and use it to estimate population parameters
We quantify our uncertainty using probability

text:
Sampling Distribution — Example







Worked Example


A population has mean \(\mu = 70\) and \(\sigma = 10\). We take samples of size \(n = 25\). Find the mean and SE of the sampling distribution.
\[\text{Mean} = \mu = 70\]
\[SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{10}{5} = 2\]
So \(\bar{x} \sim N(70,\; 2)\). Most sample means will fall between 66 and 74.

Confidence Intervals
A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter.
\[\bar{x} \pm z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Common CI levels:

90% (\(z^*=1.645\))
95% (\(z^*=1.96\))
99% (\(z^*=2.576\))

text:
Hypothesis Testing – The Big Picture
Hypothesis testing is a formal procedure to decide whether sample evidence is strong enough to reject a claim about a population.
Two Hypotheses

Null hypothesis or \(H_0\): The “nothing is happening” claim; assumed true until proven otherwise
Alternative hypothesis or \(H_a\) or \(H_1\): What we want to show; the “new” claim

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 5
text:
Setting Up Hypotheses


Two-tailed
“Is the mean different from 50?”
\[H_0: \mu = 50\] \[H_a: \mu \neq 50\]

Left-tailed
“Is the mean less than 50?”
\[H_0: \mu = 50\] \[H_a: \mu < 50\]

Right-tailed
“Is the mean greater than 50?”
\[H_0: \mu = 50\] \[H_a: \mu > 50\]







Note


The direction of \(H_a\) determines where the rejection region falls in the distribution.

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 5
text:
p-values and Significance
The p-value is the probability of getting a result as extreme as your sample, assuming \(H_0\) is true.

title: Statistics and Probability for 11th Graders - Part 5
text:
p-values and Significance
The p-value is the probability of getting a result as extreme as your sample, assuming \(H_0\) is true.


Decision Rule

If \(p\text{-value} \leq \alpha \Rightarrow \textbf{Reject } H_0\)
If \(p\text{-value} > \alpha \Rightarrow \textbf{Fail to reject } H_0\)

Common significance levels: \(\alpha = 0.05\) or \(\alpha = 0.01\)

Interpreting the p-value



p-value
Evidence against \(H_0\)




\(> 0.10\)
Weak


\(0.05 - 0.10\)
Moderate


\(0.01 - 0.05\)
Strong


\(< 0.01\)
Very strong











Important


Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\) is true – it just means there is not enough evidence to reject it.

text:
Spot the Parabola!


Before we start — where have you seen a curved, U-shaped arc in real life?


Like the path of a basketball when you throw it?

👍

Exactly! That arc is called a parabola — and today we are going to learn the equation behind it.


So quadratic equations describe that shape?


Yes. Bridges, fountains, roller coasters — they all follow the same equation: \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\).

😮

I never thought math would show up on a basketball court.


It is everywhere once you know what to look for. Let us dive in.

title: Quadratic Equations
text:
What Is a Quadratic Equation?

A quadratic equation is any equation that can be written in the form:
\[ax^2 + bx + c = 0\]
where \(a \neq 0\), and \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are real numbers.



Quadratic Examples

\(x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0\)
\(2x^2 - 3x = 0\)
\(x^2 - 9 = 0\)


NOT Quadratic

\(3x + 5 = 0\) (linear — no \(x^2\))
\(x^3 + x^2 = 0\) (cubic — degree 3)
\(\frac{1}{x} + 2 = 0\) (rational)

title: Quadratic Equations
text:
Anatomy of a Quadratic
\[\underbrace{a}_{\text{leads}}x^2 + \underbrace{b}_{\text{middle}}x + \underbrace{c}_{\text{constant}} = 0\]


Identify the values in \(3x^2 - 7x + 2 = 0\):



Part
Value




\(a\)
\(3\)


\(b\)
\(-7\)


\(c\)
\(2\)










Key Rule


The coefficient \(a\) must never equal zero. If \(a = 0\), the equation becomes linear, not quadratic.

title: Quadratic Equations
text:
Method 1: Factoring
Goal: Rewrite \(ax^2 + bx + c\) as a product of two binomials.

Example: Solve \(x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0\)
Step 1 — Find two numbers that multiply to \(c = 6\) and add to \(b = 5\):
\[\text{Factors of 6: } (1,6),\ (2,3) \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 + 3 = 5\]
Step 2 — Factor the equation:
\[(x + 2)(x + 3) = 0\]
Step 3 — Apply the Zero Product Property:
\[x + 2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = -2\] \[x + 3 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = -3\]
Solutions: \(x = -2\) or \(x = -3\)

title: Quadratic Equations
text:
Factoring Practice
Solve by factoring:
\[x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0\]

Hint: Find two numbers that multiply to \(12\) and add to \(-7\).


Answer: \((-3) \times (-4) = 12\) and \((-3) + (-4) = -7\)
\[(x - 3)(x - 4) = 0\]
\[\boxed{x = 3 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 4}\]

title: Quadratic Equations
text:
Method 2: Quadratic Formula
When factoring is difficult, we use the Quadratic Formula:

\[x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\]

This formula works for every quadratic equation.






Memory Tip


“Negative b, plus or minus square root, b squared minus 4ac, all over 2a!”

title: Quadratic Equations
text:
Quadratic Formula — Worked Example
Solve \(2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 0\)


Identify: \[a = 2, \quad b = -4, \quad c = -6\]
Substitute: \[x = \frac{-(-4) \pm \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4(2)(-6)}}{2(2)}\]
\[x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 48}}{4}\]
\[x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{64}}{4} = \frac{4 \pm 8}{4}\]

Two Solutions:
\[x = \frac{4 + 8}{4} = \frac{12}{4} = 3\]
\[x = \frac{4 - 8}{4} = \frac{-4}{4} = -1\]






Tip


\[\boxed{x = 3 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -1}\]

text:
The Discriminant
The part under the radical, \(b^2 - 4ac\), is called the discriminant \((\Delta)\).



\(\Delta > 0\)
Two real solutions
The parabola crosses the x-axis twice.



\(\Delta = 0\)
One real solution
The parabola touches the x-axis exactly once.



\(\Delta < 0\)
No real solutions
The parabola does not cross the x-axis.

Transform the equation into the form \((x + h)^2 = k\).

Quick Quiz

What are the solutions of \(x^2 - x - 6 = 0\)?


\(x = 2\) or \(x = -3\)


\(x = -2\) or \(x = 3\)


\(x = 3\) or \(x = -3\)


\(x = 1\) or \(x = -6\)




Answer: B — \(x = -2\) or \(x = 3\)
\((x - 3)(x + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 3\) or \(x = -2\)

title: Quadratic Equations

What We Learned Today


Key Takeaways

A quadratic equation has the form \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\)
We can solve by factoring, quadratic formula, or completing the square
The discriminant (\(b^2 - 4ac\)) tells us how many solutions exist
The graph of a quadratic is always a parabola
Parabolas appear everywhere in the real world








The Golden Formula


\[x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\]
Memorize this — it works every time.
